Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National US Exchange Alumni Summit: Past fellow struggle to access post-fellowship grants, limiting knowledge-transfer applications Source : Josephine Sagoe 23 November 2026 9:21pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
A 2019 Mandela Washington Fellow, Dr Joel Afi Duah, says it is becoming increasingly difficult for beneficiaries of development programs in the United States of America to access post-fellowship grants following donor cuts in the US.
Dr. Duah, who is the municipal director of Health Services for Tano South in the Ahafo Region, says the situation has limited alumni efforts to translate knowledge and skills acquired through exchange programmes into practical development projects.
He was speaking at the U.S. Embassy Ghana Exchange Alumni Summit in Kumasi.
“With the cuts in funding, alumni are leveraging their networks and available resources to sustain their work. However, it has become quite difficult to plan and execute capital projects and meet other major expenses,” he said.
He called on the government to increase funding for public institutions struggling with reductions and withdrawals in support from international development partners.
He says funding cuts by organisations, including the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the United States African Development Foundation (USADF), have disrupted development programmes and weakened the capacity of institutions and beneficiaries to sustain ongoing initiatives.
“We are therefore making a passionate appeal to the government to step up funding support in areas where donor funding has been reduced or withdrawn. This will enable us to build on the investments made and the knowledge and skills we have acquired through these fellowship programmes,” he asserted.
Dr Duah believes increased government investment will be critical to sustaining the gains made through international partnerships and ensuring that development initiatives do not stall because of funding constraints.
The appeal comes as the U.S. Embassy in Ghana brings together about 100 alumni of U.S. government exchange programmes from the Ashanti Region and Ghana’s middle belt for an Alumni Excellence Summit in Kumasi.
The event, held on Saturday, November 21, 2026, celebrated the contributions of former exchange programme participants to national development across various sectors.
It also forms part of activities marking the 250th anniversary of American independence under the Freedom 250 initiative.
Cultural Affairs Attaché at the U.S. Embassy in Ghana, Donya Eldridge, said the exchange programmes are intended to promote knowledge-sharing and expose participants to approaches the US has adopted in addressing development challenges that Ghana also faces.
“Our alumni include students and professionals who have had the opportunity to learn from experiences in the United States. The idea is to share what they have done, the lessons they have learned, and help us understand how similar approaches can work in the Ghanaian economy,” she stated.
